utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. First of all, I'd like to welcome the representatives of UNMIK and I would like -- I would invite them introduce themselves. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My name is Alexander Borg-Olivier, I'm the legal advisor for UNMIK in the office of the SRSG.

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Annunziata Ciaravolo, I am the deputy director, department of justice and chief international prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Ciaravolo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALTON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honour. My name is Nathan Dalton, I'm the special assistant to the director of the department of justice, UNMIK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dalton. This morning we have not the hearing as usual hearing testimony, but the Chamber has invited UNMIK for two reasons. First of all, the Chamber would like to be informed in more detail about the concerns UNMIK apparently has in giving its consent for disclosure of certain material provided confidentially to the Prosecution. And the second purpose is to see whether the matter can be resolved in one way or another. The issue has been raised by Mr. Guy-Smith in a motion of the 12th of January of this year. I understand that the UNMIK representatives have had an opportunity to look at the transcripts where the matter was discussed and that also the parties have been kind enough to provide you with correspondence they exchanged on the matter. I do understand that UNMIK has, until now, given its consent for disclosure of quite a number of pages of two investigation files but not for all of them. And the major point of concern is that the Prosecution has informed this Chamber that among the non-disclosed pages there are 16 pages which contain exculpatory material. I'm always a bit hesitant to say "exculpatory material." Some would say potential exculpatory material, but if we define exculpatory material in accordance with the text of Rule 68, then the potentiality is already included in the definition because Rule 68(i) says: "... material which in the actual knowledge of the Prosecutor may suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence." The problem for the Chamber is the following. If there exists material of an exculpatory nature which the Chamber is unaware of, this creates a risk that we might make a mistake in whatever determinations we make. That's one. On the other hand, if we would just order disclosure of this material, then from the UNMIK's missions I do understand that they do not exclude that the Chamber may have the authority to do so. But if we would too easily do that, we might disencourage entities or persons at a later stage to provide relevant information under Rule 70. So the Chamber has to find a fair balance between not discouraging anyone to provide information to the Tribunal, even if it would be on a confidential basis; and at the same time to guaranty that the trial against the three accused in this case is still fair. That's our problem. And the first issue the Chamber would like to raise is we would like to invite UNMIK where UNMIK has expressed, as far as we understand until now, that a redaction of the material would not sufficiently serve the -- or meet the concerns of UNMIK. Whether UNMIK has further examined the material and whether there are any alternatives for providing the relevant information and at the same time not violating or not -- in a way not prejudicial to perhaps the witnesses. The Chamber of course doesn't know what the material is, whether these are reports, whether these are testimonies or statements of witnesses. So first of all I'd like to invite UNMIK to further inform the Chamber about the efforts made until now and whether UNMIK has considered any alternatives apart from full disclosure or partial disclosure of the 16 pages we are talking about. We started in open session. If at any moment the UNMIK representatives would consider it appropriate that the public would not be informed about the information UNMIK wants to provide to the Chamber, you may apply for private session, which means that whatever you say at that moment will not be disclosed to the public. Of course everyone in this courtroom would hear what you say. If at a certain moment UNMIK would consider it necessary to address the Chamber in the absence of the parties, please indicate so. This is not to say that the Chamber will then grant that immediately. The Chamber might want to hear from the parties whether the parties would agree with such a procedure, but at least tell us if there are any such wishes. Mr. Borg-Olivier, could you please respond to my invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may, I would like to start with a general kind of statement, where I would state that UNMIK of course fully recognises its responsibility to assist the ICTY and its processes in every way it can. This is an obligation that it has stemming from the resolutions establishing the Tribunal and of course from the resolutions establishing UNMIK as the interim administration in Kosovo and also under our applicable law, this is reflected in our applicable law. As you know, Your Honour, we have received and you have recognised this, several requests for assistance in the vicinity of about 100, and we have I think established a clear record of constructive cooperation. Yes, we recognise that there are some difficulties and differences in the interpretation of the respective roles and responsibilities, but we do recognise fully the need to allow the Prosecution to evaluate any exculpatory evidentiary material, and where this is indicated, provided certain conditions are satisfied from UNMIK's policy perspective, and that means normally we need to know that a particular witness is indicated to participate in the proceeding, a particular witness has indicated a willingness to cooperate in the process, and this then is evaluated very carefully to see whether we are in a position to provide full disclosure or disclosure under certain conditions that take into account our public policy, responsibilities for safety and security in Kosovo and, of course, the overriding consideration of safety and absence of any intimidation that could arise for witnesses. So we would like to ensure that if we agree to disclosure, we know exactly what the information is needed for and then we try our very best to cooperate to provide as constructive and as broad a response as possible. I believe that we have indicated on various occasions that we are ready to provide redacted versions of statements that are required, where all the conditions are not fully met for full disclosure. And we understand that on occasions the redacted material that we are ready to provide is either considered not to be sufficient or not to be of sufficient evidentiary value. I will ask the acting director of justice maybe to assist in answering the second part of the question as to what are alternatives that we have considered. We -- I know we have in our responses always acknowledged that at the end of the day the ultimate authority rests with the Trial Chamber, and of course the Trial Chamber could indicate by its orders that certain material should be disclosed under the conditions that the Trial Chamber, we trust, would set out. So there's no question about that. But under Rule 70, we do consider that UNMIK as the interim administration authority has the rights -- the same rights as a state and that if it is going to disclose material that it considers could give rise to serious security concerns, these concerns need to be brought to the attention of the Trial Chamber so that they can be properly evaluated before any final decision is taken. So thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps I can ask my colleague Annunziata Ciaravolo to maybe indicate what efforts we have made to meet the needs for disclosure in the absence of the ability to provide full disclosure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to add that generally speaking, as a policy, when we are going to disclose, for example, statements given by witnesses, as a policy with the OTP we indicate that we indicate that we need the consent of the witnesses. And when we get and OTP get the consent, we are ready to provide full disclosure and we did it several times. In the case in question now in presence of the parties we can say that the witnesses didn't consent to the disclosure, so this is the reason why at the moment we have consented only for disclosure with conditions. So if it is necessary to provide additional details, I would suggest probably to be allowed to continue in only -- without the presence of the parties, because our concern still exists considering that the witnesses didn't consent to the full disclosure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we -- before I invite the parties to express themselves on your request for in camera hearing, I'd like to know a bit more what we are actually talking about without disclosing names of witnesses or positions witnesses may have held. Let me try to explain what I mean. Exculpatory material can be in a wide range going from family circumstances of an accused which might lead to a milder sentence up to - and let's just look at what this case is about. I do understand that the 16 pages are part of two files, CCIU 2002 00172 and same number but then the last five digits 00080. This Chamber was informed that it deals with the fate of a certain Mr. Skender Kuci and we have received evidence on Mr. Skender Kuci. Now, for example, to just give you an impression of the range of exculpatory material that I could imagine. We do understand that there are some medical reports saying that Mr. Kuci finally was hospitalised with at least problems with the functioning of both kidneys. Now, it could be exculpatory, for example, to have a medical record of previous kidney problems Mr. Kuci may have had because that might change the interpretation of what finally caused the death of Mr. Kuci. Was that a pre-existing condition or was it for other reasons, bad treatment in prison, beatings -- well, it could be anything. But at least that would be exculpatory material which sheds some light on the events. Of course there is other information, other material imaginable, such as a witness saying that he knew the persons who abducted Mr. Kuci and these were certainly not KLA soldiers but FARK soldiers or Serb policemen, I do not know. That's of course a kind of exculpatory material which is totally different in the range from the first example I gave. Now, the Chamber has got no idea whatsoever what the exculpatory material is. And it might be relevant for us to know a bit more about the kind of information before we proceed in excluding parties from this hearing. Is it eye-witness of an abduction? Is it medical information? Is it imprisonment conditions? It could be anything. So before we proceed - and if need be, we could go into private session - the Chamber would like to get at least some general impression of what type of material we are talking about and invites UNMIK or the Prosecution, after having consulted UNMIK, to at least give a glimpse of an impression what we are talking about. Is there any way to do that, whether in private session or in public session? Yes, Mr. Borg-Olivier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The other microphone, please, to be switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: I mean, in principle we want to be as cooperative and to provide and disclose as much as possible. Let's start from that premise. And the only time that UNMIK has withheld full disclosure, it is based on always the possible threats to a witness or serious security considerations that could arise from disclosure of particular materials. So certainly I don't think that we would not find a way to disclose exculpatory materials of the nature that you described, Your Honour, relating to medical records and the like. I think that we are much, much more concerned where the material that is being sought could implicate individuals, persons who do not wish to be connected with the proceedings, and therefore we have to exercise our responsibilities and indicate caveats which are not insurmountable. We usually indicate the caveats to the Office of the Prosecution, and we always indicate that we are ready to provide alternatives to full disclosure. And maybe we should work harder that -- to ensure that these alternatives nevertheless provide sufficient value for purposes that the information is requiring. But perhaps I can ask Ms. Ciaravolo to explain a little bit more on the types of concerns that the department of justice focuses on. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I do understand your concerns; there's no problem about that. But at the same time, first of all, of course in most legal systems it's considered a civil obligation to assist in -- as a witness in proceedings. So the starting point is not in most systems whether someone wants to be involved but whether there are -- whether the person is needed to do justice. And then second, if there are reasons to make an exception to this general rule. So the starting point might be different. That doesn't say that the final result would -- might be the same, but the starting point of reasoning is certainly different from what you've just said, for us at least. And second, if I ask you to give the type of information, we should clearly distinguish between source and the substance. At this moment I'm looking for substance rather than for source. For example, if it would be medical information, I would at this moment not be interested in whether the general practitioner would have provided information, perhaps even against his duties on an earlier pre-existing kidney condition, or if it is about prison. I'm not interested to know whether the neighbours of a prison or guards in a prison or other detainees in that same prison gave the information, but I'd like to know whether the confidential information is about medical condition, prison conditions, ill-treatment, transportation, whether it is about -- well, whatever. I'm talking about a general impression on the substance of the exculpatory material. Ms. Ciaravolo, if you could respond to this, you're invited to do so. And if you would rather -- of course, it might be a bit difficult for UNMIK to know exactly what is exculpatory because that also depends on the evidence and on the charges before this Chamber. So therefore, if you'd like to consult with Mr. Re and authorise him to give such a general impression, you're invited to do so. I leave it up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to say that we have two witnesses who gave statements related to information to the witnesses by someone else who saw this other person, saw the incident in question. So these witnesses were not present at the time of the alleged abduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: Then we have another witness, and this witness was not a physician and did not conduct any physical examination of the victim, but had only the possibility to see the victim at a certain point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps with your permission I could add that in direct response to your comment as to the substance of the material, I can say with confidence that UNMIK would find always to release information relating to substance. That does not necessarily sort of touch source and implicate parties, because as you said, this is of secondary importance. What's important is the substantive value of information that could be exculpatory. As to whether something is exculpatory or not, we first, of course, at UNMIK receive requests for information from the Office of the Prosecutor, and it is in our view their responsibility to extract any possible exculpatory materials from the materials that we provide. And if it is indicated to us that in the view of the Office of the Prosecutor there may be exculpatory material, that does not necessarily mean that we are in agreement that what we are about to provide is, in fact, exculpatory. And we must leave that for further evaluation, including from -- by the Trial Chamber, and we have expressed our readiness to make available information and then we leave it to the Court to make a final determination as to whether material is, in fact, exculpatory. We are not always convinced with the indications that material may be -- is potentially exculpatory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, that's the primary responsibility of the Prosecution. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence impose some obligations on the Prosecution how to act if there's exculpatory material. So it's finally -- it's the assessment, of course to be verified by the Chamber if need be, it's the assessment of the Prosecution, first of all, to identify material as exculpatory. So I do understand now we are talking about witnesses who gave hearsay evidence, hearsay evidence of a third person who has observed the abduction. Is it limited to the abduction or is it more widely on what happened after the abduction?

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: I would like to maybe just clarify my previous statement. Regarding the person who was present at the incident, the statement given by this witness were unconditionally released. Just for clarification. So the hearsay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the -- the substance --

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: The substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of the hearsay information --

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- has been released.

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: Has been completely released, because the witness present agreed and the statements were unconditionally released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the only thing we are talking about is that other witnesses who confirm --

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the fact -- well, do not confirm but that other witnesses who have stated that the witness who observed the abduction, which is available material, that this witness had told them that he observed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then of course the next issue would be whether the information these two witnesses received from the third person who observed the abduction, whether there's any inconsistency between what this witness told them and what we find in the statement of that witness. Therefore, I would be inclined to seek a solution in the following direction; that is, to perhaps have disclosed the substance of the hearsay evidence to the extent where it states what these witnesses heard from the third person who observed the abduction and to see whether there's any inconsistency. If there's any inconsistency, then of course this might shed some light on the probative value, on the reliability of the information the witness gave in a statement which is available to the parties. Perhaps we leave it for a second in relation to this material to this, because I'm looking at the Defence whether the Defence would consider that a solution might be at least provisionally, initially sought in that direction. And I saw that there was some consultation between Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I was, in fact, having a word with Mr. Guy-Smith primarily on the procedural aspect; in other words, whether it would and in what circumstances it would be appropriate to -- to consent to the suggestion that had been made that the Trial Chamber be addressed in the absence of the parties, and I have some submissions at the appropriate moment to make in that direction. But I don't understand Your Honour to be asking me that question at this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not at this moment. As you may have noticed, the Chamber was not very much inclined to immediately --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- respond to that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And the short response to the question would the substance be of advantage to the parties is: Plainly it would be. The more information that one can have, the better position the parties will be in to make informed submissions about relevance and probative value. And indeed a situation could arise, one can imagine and I've seen it in other contexts, where the substance of the information itself, without the identification of the provider, can become part of the record with the Tribunal making certain assumptions about the probative weight of it. And it can be deployed, in certain circumstances, without necessarily full identification having been properly explored. But clearly if we're proceeding in stages to disclose to the Defence at this stage the substance would be of very considerable assistance, providing one knows in that particular instance who the maker of the statement to the person who is the author of the UNMIK statement was. In other words, in order to identify the possibility of inconsistency one has to know which eye-witness provided the account to the two hearsay witnesses in order to be able to compare it with what we understand to be a statement that has already been disclosed from an eye-witness. But that is, I wouldn't have thought, likely to represent a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore I understand there are two important elements. The first is to identify what is the -- who is the third person who observed the abduction, so in order to enable you to compare if the substance of the hearsay statement is released.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In that particular instance -- there is a more general proposition that ought perhaps just to be recorded at this point, which is, there's been some discussion about whether material is or is not exculpatory, what the test is, whose responsibility it is, and so forth. I do think it's important to record at this stage that not only in respect of these requests, but more generally in respect of any specific requests made by the Defence which are in fact requests made under 66(B) rather than 68, the threshold test must be relevance. If material is relevant, then it's prima facie disclosable in the absence of a strong public interest against its disclosure. And really the question of whether it's exculpatory or not or how exculpatory it is only becomes material when a Court is called upon to perform a balance between the public interest in disclosure and the public interest in nondisclosure. And deciding whether material is exculpatory or not or, indeed, deciding how exculpatory it is is not a process that UNMIK can perform, because they don't know what lines of cross-examination we may wish to pursue; neither, with the greatest of respect, is it a function that the Prosecution can perform on our behalf. The only people who are properly fit to decide or at least to assess in the first instance potential value are the Defence and then ultimately the Trial Chamber and to make that evaluation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, that's fine in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we are faced here with a very specific situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where Rule 70 leaves it to the provider of the material to say no, and the only issue is whether the Chamber is competent to; and if so, should give an order that Rule 68 would prevail. Against the text of Rule 68 --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which starts saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Subject to Rule 70."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Subject to Rule 70." So I would like to focus on that issue because that's the central issue raised in the January motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And may I say I fully accept that that creates a balancing exercise which is circumscribed, but nonetheless when the balancing exercise comes to be performed, for the Trial Chamber to be able to decide how valuable a piece of material may be, which is obviously critical to deciding whether a Rule 70 document should be the subject of an order, assuming the Trial Chamber has power to order its disclosure, how useful it is to the Defence is clearly one of the most important factors that the Trial Chamber will have to consider. And for that to occur, the Trial Chamber must be equipped with informed submissions from the Defence, and they cannot be equipped with informed submissions from the Defence about how useful a document may be if the parties are excluded from the process at any stage. That was really the point. So some solution would have to be devised to enable informed submissions to be made by the Defence as to the weight or potential value of Rule 70 material, which raises the balancing exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson, I was focusing at this moment mainly on trying to find a solution which would meet both UNMIK concerns and Defence concerns, and you already started a bit giving the general context and the general matters. As a matter of fact, I, not without reason, started not on the abstract level but first on the practical level because if -- of course, in the back of the minds of the Chamber - and the Chamber has thoroughly discussed the matter - all the balancing exercises, all the interests involved, but the Chamber tries to focus at this moment to see whether we can resolve the matter, as I said at the beginning, to be informed and to seek a resolution. If no resolution could be found here, then of course the Chamber will have to consider how to finally decide on the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I could simply have said the suggestion is a helpful one and, yes, I would like to see the substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to at this point forego discussion of the law, and I think there is some well-settled law in certain of these areas, and suggest that the Chamber's suggestion is the one that we should follow at this time because I think there is a practical solution therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- so therefore, Mr. Re, you heard the Defence. We now have at least some indication of at least a part of it because we have dealt only with the first issue, that is the two hearsay witnesses, where a provisional solution might be found by, first of all, informing the Defence on the substance of the hearsay without giving any sources; it's not Witness A or Witness B or Witness C, but there are two witnesses saying that they were told by a third person, who observed the abduction, the following. And then it's mainly the substance, the content of what he states or the two witnesses state they've heard from this person. That's one portion. The second is that the Defence is informed about the source of knowledge for these two hearsay witnesses so that they can compare the statement given by that witness and the statement about receiving information from that witness by the two unidentified witnesses. Would that for the time being be the first step in reaching a solution? Mr. Re, you have been silent until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, yes. I just wish to make a comment here about the submissions of UNMIK to date. There are two matters with which the Prosecution -- we're not quite sure about the accuracy of part of the submissions. The first one is at page 5 where Mr. Borg-Olivier referred to UNMIK - I'll just find the passage - where he said: "I believe that we have indicated on various occasions that we are ready to provide redacted versions of statements that are required" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To keep matters short, it's my memory that at some point the Chamber was informed that there was a major concern about giving redacted statements because it would still identify the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The only point I wish to make there is that UNMIK have said that they have offered -- or were ready to provide redacted statements. And if I could just refer the Trial Chamber to our filing of the 17th of November, 2005, and the provisional release litigation, paragraph 44, where we said we had actually offered that to UNMIK, but UNMIK had declined our invitation to do it in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- that's the past, I would say. And if there's any need to further discuss whether the communication up till this very moment was not perfect, then I gladly leave it in the hands of those who participated in that communication to express their views, not necessarily in this courtroom. But I do understand that you do not fully agree with the presentation given by Mr. Borg-Olivier on the history of the matter. At this moment I'm not saying that it lacks all relevance for this Chamber, but we are not focusing on it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What we are focusing on - and I of course take Your Honour's direction here - is the substance of what is contained in the files which we have. Mr. Borg-Olivier says there are three -- two statements. Our understanding, based on our requests and correspondences, that there are three statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. While we have -- I only dealt with the first issue, that is two unidentified witnesses gave a statement, a hearsay statement, on what a third person said. But we have another that is someone who saw the victim. We have not dealt with that yet, if that's the third. If not, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. What I'm trying to come to is I'm not quite sure who they're talking about. If they can give me the names on a piece of paper, then I'll know if their information is the same as ours. The reason is this -- if Your Honour will let me say this, the reason is the information I have in the file is that it is not hearsay. There are two witnesses and I don't think we've ever said they are hearsay witnesses. So there appears to be a discrepancy there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion which --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If they can put the names on a piece of paper and just hand them to me, I can work out straight away who they're talking about and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Ciaravolo, would that be a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the interim and really quite briefly, since Mr. Re has raised the issue of provisional release, and I quite frankly don't want to get off on a point of law at this time because I think we're trying to at least for these purposes on this issue reach a practical solution. The use of that material in the provisional release does raise some other legal issues with regard to what, if any, protections it has, having been initially supplied under Rule 70. And I'm just making a footnote of that for the moment because if that becomes an issue at a later point in time, depending on how much time we have for these proceedings, the Chamber may need to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do we need at this moment -- is the information of UNMIK relevant for that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Only because it -- only -- it may well be, and this is really an issue that I think more appropriately might be dealt with by Mr. Harvey at a point in time when he addresses the Chamber with regard to the provision of material as it related to the provisional release by UNMIK. It's an entirely separate issue, but since it was raised, I just want to make sure that the Court is aware that there is a--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's actually a tertiary legal issue, which we don't need to get into it at this point but I don't want to lose sight of it in the event it becomes of some moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That brings me to some thoughts which I will express at a later stage. Mr. Re, are you talking about the same statements as UNMIK did?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, if I can correct myself it does appear to be hearsay. I just misread something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that issue is resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So we are talking about the same thing. And the Prosecution doesn't object to the suggestion the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So the suggestion is -- just dealing with the first piece of information, is that the substance of the hearsay, without saying who said it, but at least the statement to the extent it relates the information these hearsay witnesses received from the third persons are disclosed to the Defence, and also to the extent that does not yet appear clearly from those statements who the witness is who personally observed the abduction. So that there is impossibility to compare.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the suggestion is not problematic at all for UNMIK. If we could propose an appropriate redaction, that meets those requirements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll then see once this has been disclosed whether there were any further concerns. I hardly could imagine that the Defence would have no further concerns, but then of course the next step would be to consider whether there needs additional steps. Now I'd like to move to the second piece of information where you said there is a witness statement of a person who saw the victim. Now, relying on -- relying on the evidence we've heard until now and also looking at the indictment, it might be relevant to know whether the victim was seen by the witness when he was still alive or after he died and whether he was seen only after he had died or only when still alive. Is that -- is this a kind of information you could provide to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Again, I think that this could be addressed and can be satisfactory to a redaction of the information to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could you inform us on whether -- I mean, what are we talking about, I mean, if it would have been his -- well, let's say the witness could be -- one of his children stating about his physical condition after the body was delivered to the family, that's of course totally different from someone who sees the condition of the victim when transported --

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from a detention facility to a hospital, for example. Could you -- is there any way in general terms to give a bit more information about --

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: I'll ask Ms. Ciaravolo to be maybe specific. I don't wish to get into the actual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: -- evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if there's need, Ms. Ciaravolo, to go into private session, you'll let me know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We can say that this person was at the hospital when the victim was still alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And also at the hospital when the victim had died?

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: This, I can't say. I don't -- she later heard that he died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CIARAVOLO
utterances.text: She or he.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can imagine, looking at material which is not in evidence but which was in the bundle the Chamber received recently, that there would be a need to compare the medical information the Defence has given to the Chamber, these were reports about the possible causes of this kidney failure, with this information. I do not know at this moment to what extent that material would be exculpatory, but here again the substance of the information, without saying whether it was a visitor or a nurse or a doctor, at the same time of course, sometimes the Chamber is aware that if it comes to the substance of information, if it is described in rather medical terms, then you could expect that there was a medical professional involved. So to that extent it would identify at least some of the -- would give some information about --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I just add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- on that one point. Your Honour should be aware - and I'm sure UNMIK are aware - that in the file in addition to the statement and medical report that Your Honours have seen, there is another statement and medical report from another doctor less directly involved, which is essentially consistent with the one that Your Honours have seen. But in that second statement, there is a list of the names of all of the medical staff. I'm simply saying that because it is obviously relevant if names are in issue, because as soon as one were able to identify the -- as soon as the capacity in which a member of the medical team involved is revealed, that is -- will come in substance to the revelation of the identity because the list is already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The material you're talking about, is that all material disclosed by the Prosecution to the Defence or is there any material generated by the Defence itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The answer to that question comes in two stages. I think the answer that Your Honour needs is the list of names comes from material disclosed by the Prosecution from the UNMIK file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again going for a practical solution, would -- as a first step, would it meet some of the concerns of the Defence if the substance of the information provided by a person who has seen the victim in the hospital would be disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harvey, unisono yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I continue to nod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you continue to nod. Mr. Re, any comment on --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's not our file. We don't object to that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I do -- but nevertheless you are a participant in these proceedings as well, so I'd like to hear your opinion about the matter. Would it be practical to -- I don't know how much time it takes to -- perhaps with a marker to get rid of all the information and then perhaps just show it to the Defence for the time being so that we could use 25 minutes to see how far we come and see whether any additional steps are needed? That brings me to another matter which I'd like to raise and that is direct communication between UNMIK and Defence. I do understand that the communication, direct communication, between Defence and UNMIK sometimes finds an obstacle in the preference of UNMIK to deal with the Defence rather through the Prosecution. I would like to invite UNMIK to reconsider whether this indirect communication is always the exclusively appropriate way of dealing with parties in these proceedings. And just perhaps to give it a start, if you have provisionally redacted these statements, I would invite you to meet with the Defence, to show it to them, and to see whether at that moment there's any need to seek further clarifications, not to engage in a real discussion on the matter. But, for example, if the Defence would say, I see a redacted page 2 and a redacted page 4, is there any page 3? Is it not relevant, or are you just -- have you just forgotten to look at page 3 or is the numbering in this file incomplete? These kind of practical communication often helps a lot in resolving matters. So perhaps in this relatively safe environment you could perhaps try it out once whether direct communication with lead counsel would favour finding of a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, your wise comments are duly noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: And I assure you that starting from the end of your remarks, UNMIK's position is not exclusively to deal with the Office of the Prosecutor alone. As a matter of policy - and I think this is appreciated and understood - as an interim administration authority we must be sure that we are always dealing with an official process that has the full cognizance of the Tribunal. And so as a matter of policy, we state that we deal in matters relating to the ICTY with the competent ICTY authorities, and that is the registry, it is the Chamber, and it is the OTP. And we don't respond directly, as a matter of policy, to Defence counsel that come from all angles and with issues that might not be in the best interest of anyone to go forward with before getting a view from the competent authorities of ICTY that this is something that is necessary and useful that we should cooperate with. And we have had communications with Defence counsel on various occasions, and in the manner that you have described, we certainly don't see a problem after the initial issues of principle have been determined. Thereafter we could still -- we could have definitely informal exchanges with Defence on what we have been able to disclose, for instance. If we disclose a redacted statement and there are questions on the redaction, I don't see that there should be any difficulty in clarifications, direct clarifications being exchanged between Defence and UNMIK. But it is our very firm policy and -- that we do not respond directly or disclose directly to Defence counsel. We have up to now adhered to a policy of insisting that we receive requests for assistance from the competent organs of the ICTY; we respond; and then we are ready to enter into a dialogue as to how much of that can be disclosed if it's necessary, if any clarifications are required. I don't know if I've been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've been clear enough. It might need, perhaps, some further discussions on the role of Defence and Prosecution as parties in proceedings, especially in these proceedings with an adversarial character where, unlike in many non-adversarial systems, the Defence has a duty and is expected to find its own material, and where it might not always be fair that when the Defence is seeking some material, to first give it in the hands of the Prosecution, whereas if the Prosecution seeks some material, it does not pass the hands of the Defence. So perhaps, but not at this moment, an exchange of views on the characteristics of the adversarial proceedings might be useful to see whether your policy is -- is in every respect fair to all parties in these proceedings. But we are not engaging in that discussion at this moment, but since you mentioned it, I give -- and I say not the view of the Chamber but my personal view on the matter you just raised. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since that issue has been raised, I hope that we will be able to come to some form of resolution because of the fact that at this point in time the numbers of requests that are outstanding are legion and it's quite clear to me that the position of UNMIK has not deviated from its February 12th, 2007, position, which is the obligation to disclose evidence belongs exclusively to the ICTY Prosecutor. I hope that by the end of today's proceedings we will be able to reach some form of resolution on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Guy-Smith, this Chamber is not in the position to dictate the policy of UNMIK. Of course in an exchange of views, whether in the context of this case or whether in more general context, might assist in considering, as I said before, whether this policy in every respect is fair to all parties in these proceedings, that might be the positive approach to what you consider to be a policy problem and what UNMIK considers policy. And whether that would change or not change, the policy is not the primary concern of this Chamber; but of course, if the Defence seeks information where the Prosecution would not support such a request, of course the Defence can -- but then on an ad hoc basis, invite the Chamber to give an order to UNMIK to disclose certain material to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that and am attempting to do everything to avoid that situation because the number of orders that we would be requesting thus far, based upon the position that the Office of the Prosecutor has taken, is such that we will reach that position if we don't - and I hope that we do come to some form of accord - we will reach that position very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you will, since UNMIK is there, a conversation on the matter might be possible, even using the presence of the UNMIK representatives. Mr. Borg-Olivier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just on a point about the February 12th response, I mean, that response is in the context of information provided to the OTP. And in respect of that information, there's no doubt in our minds that it is for the OTP to make its evaluations and decide what it should disclose to the Defence. But there are other situations where, clearly, there needs to be some involvement between the Defence and the material; and this we would certainly be open to any arrangement that this Tribunal would indicate that involved perhaps the Tribunal, through the Chamber. If the Chamber, as is being done in this particular case, we have seen the wisdom of referring the matter to the Chamber and the Chamber is giving us guidance as to how to overcome an obstacle that overcomes difficulties that the parties legitimately have from their different perspectives. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would -- the policy of this Chamber is that we are always trying to see whether the parties can resolve their problems themselves; and only if that's impossible, to ask the Chamber to intervene. Let's not -- as I said in the beginning, we are trying to find practical solutions rather than to have legal debates on, although of course all being lawyers we like legal debates but we'd rather first resolve our problems that come up in our efforts to provide a fair trial to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The -- I'm only rising to correct the representation just made. The letter that I alluded to was in direct response to two requests that I made specifically to UNMIK that I had not made to the Office of the Prosecutor because I was informed in one instance that the Office of the Prosecutor would not be in a position to do so; and in the other instance it was a situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I see that you have concern a bit similar to a concern expressed by Mr. Re previously, and I would say, as I did encourage further direct communication to resolve all misunderstandings, misinterpretations, et cetera, I again encourage you to engage in direct conversations to see whether you can resolve these matters. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe as a proposal or a compromise, the Prosecution - I just place this on the record - we do not view ourselves and we are not -- our role is not that of a collection agency for the Defence and we're not -- we will not act as the Defence's agent in collecting information from [sic] the Defence. We make that quite clear, we have no obligation to do so. There are some cases in which we have made requests of UNMIK when the Defence has asked us to do so. That has been on a case-by-case basis where we have considered it to be in the interests of justice, as we see it, to do so. Now, we hear what UNMIK is saying here in relation to what they see as the official organs of the Tribunal. If it's not us and they're not going to communicate with the Defence and we can't do anything about that, the compromise solution may be through a third party, possibly the registry. If they direct their requests to the registry -- the Defence requests them to the registry and the registry to UNMIK and it goes back through the registry to UNMIK to the Defence, it keeps the Prosecution out of it, would allay Your Honour's concerns about the fairness of the process and the two parties would be communicating without involving the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see there are all possible thoughts on how to resolve the matter, and the Chamber is confident that at least the first problems might be resolved in the half an hour we'll take for a break. The Chamber is not ordering who should provide coffee to who, but we would like to see you back at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to hear the result of the meeting between Defence and UNMIK during the break, whether it has at least initially resolved the outstanding issue of information as we discussed before the break. Mr. Guy-Smith, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, I would, on behalf of the Defence, and I think really on behalf of all parties, thank the Chamber for the suggestions made and the invitation for us to have these discussions because I think they've been really quite fruitful and I believe that we at least at the outset have come up with a solution. There may be a point or two which needs to be ironed out, but in principle without any doubts I think it would be fair to say that we have come up with an accord that should work for all parties. Initially with regard to the issue of the statements that were the first part of the subject of the Court, we have received redacted copies of those statements. They are in the process of being reviewed at this point in time, and I think we'll be able to very shortly report back to the Chamber with regard to whether or not we will need any further information or not. I can take it no further than that, only because they are being reviewed by all parties at this point. With regard to the second issue, which is the issue of requests that the Defence might need to make or will be making in terms of information that is within the possession, custody, and control of UNMIK in the nature of investigative files and/or exculpatory information, we have, I think it would be fair to say, have agreed in principle, that we - meaning the Defence - at this time can directly contact a designated member of UNMIK with regard to a request for that information which we deem to be relevant for the adequate and proper preparation of the defence of our clients. UNMIK, I believe, is in a position where they will be able to respond to those requests; however, they have made a request that there is some interim, either approval or noting by some agency or organ of the Tribunal that indicates that the requests are bona fide and kosher, that perhaps is a way of putting it. How precisely to achieve that particular part of the process has yet to be ironed out and perhaps the Chamber might have some ideas. I think that I've fairly indicated. There is an area that might arise where certain information is information which UNMIK believes should be kept confidential, but there are ways of alerting both the Defence as well as the Office of the Prosecutor to any of those situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Borg-Olivier, first of all, could you confirm that Mr. Guy-Smith gave a fair reflection of your conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, by and large, the account is fair and comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then he also announced that UNMIK might have some, as he said, a kind of an approval or at least a notice that, as Mr. Guy-Smith said, the request was bona fide or kosher. Could you explain what UNMIK would like in this respect and we might then discuss this issue to see whether we can reach a conclusion on that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, we had fruitful discussions during the break, and UNMIK, as I said earlier, has consistently adhered to a policy of requiring some involvement or oversight by the Tribunal authorities of any action that is presented to UNMIK for some kind of response. And in keeping with this, we recognise that there are times we need to help the Defence, and we want to simply be sure that a request coming to UNMIK has at least the official oversight of the ICTY competent authorities. This could be the registry, it could be the Chamber that designates a focal point. All that is needed that there be some kind of stamp, official stamp, showing that this has passed through an official office, and then we know that if there's any reason why the Tribunal does not want us to act on it, then we wouldn't. If there is no objection sort of then we would proceed to deal with it as a request that the Tribunal knows about and that we feel we should respond to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may ask a few questions in that respect. You said it has passed through an official office and then we know if there's any reason why the Tribunal does not want us to act on it, then we wouldn't -- if there is no objection, then we would proceed. What would you expect, whether it's the registry or the Chamber, for us -- what would be our considerations or what would be our criteria for saying this should not reacted to or not. Because in the adversarial system the Chamber - but the same would be true for the registry - is usually not interfering or even seeking information on how the parties prepare their case, how they do their discovery. So therefore, if I would have to look at it, should I close my eyes and say "approved," or what do you expect us, apart from the -- of course it's always nice to have a stamp on a document, but what do you expect us to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Well, maybe I went too far, Your Honour, in saying if there is any objection it should be indicated. Maybe one should not go down that route and simply acknowledge that, yes, in the adversarial system, really this is not something that should be sort of looked into more than simply to acknowledge that it has passed through an official channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: And if we have, let's say, a stamp, then we know that this has been officially noted and recorded and we have it -- and we're not the only ones that have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: And if, for instance, a request has been made that has been covered amply through other disclosures, perhaps either we could get some guidance and assistance that this is the case or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this Chamber is not aware of disclosure. I mean, the parties have disclosure obligations. The Chamber usually asks the parties, Are you happy -- is the Defence happy with the way the Prosecution has fulfilled its disclosure obligations? If they say yes, we are not going to ask. Of course if it comes to trial - but that's of course a different matter - if it will be presented as evidence then of course it reaches the Chamber, but all that material reviewed by Defence or Prosecution which never comes to our eyes, we are unaware of it. And in the system, it's normal that we are unaware of it. But I do understand some concern, for example, that if there would later be any debate about whether a request has been made. Let me also see whether there's a practical solution. If a party would make a request, first send it to the Legal Officer of the Chamber, the Legal Officer being authorised by the Chamber to sign that he has received a copy which is to be stored until there will be any dispute about this request, would that do?

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask parties, especially the Defence, whether that could resolve the matter. Of course it would -- it would need your confidence that the Chamber is not going to review in detail -- of course we might ask our Legal Officers, How many requests were there last month? 25? 100? 200? But the Chamber of course sees the concerns of UNMIK, that at least it's recorded somewhere, apart from in your files. And in a fundamental discussion, it might be that we would take the position that storing the original in the files of the Defence would be just as good, but if the Defence would not oppose against this solution, then we might consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't oppose against the solution because I think that the main effect of it will be to achieve that which is most important to us, which is the receipt of the information, and I am confident that the Chamber has more than enough work in front of it that it doesn't need to be going through necessarily the requests that are being made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's clear for UNMIK that the Chamber will not review whether we find it serious or not. If there's any reason for UNMIK why they would not be willing to provide the information, of course I take it that the next step from the Defence would be to -- either to ask the Chamber to make an invitation, but then at least we have differentiated between those cases where there are special concerns by UNMIK which causes UNMIK not to be cooperative at that instance, and then of course we could, upon an application by the Defence, we could consider whether there's any reason to send you an invitation, having heard both Defence and UNMIK, whether there's any reason to apply Rule 54 bis, which is a possibility for a state to say, We would like to address the Chamber in camera because we have very special concerns that should not be brought to the attention, then you're even entitled under the Rules to bring your own interpreters so that even not by the interpreters any information could leak. It's really then just the state or, in this case, UNMIK. If that practical solution, which your request for a rubber stamp is not acknowledged as being valid but is accepted as a practical solution to meet your concerns, it doesn't say anything about whether the Chamber considers this necessary and whether your obligation under Article 29 of the Statute and whether the presumption in Rule 54 bis that the parties just directly deal with the entity concerned, whether we would share your views that such a stamp would be needed. There has been quite some case law in this respect, not only in relation to states but also in relation to NATO or the European Monitoring Mission which all start from the assumption that reasonable requests by parties, whether Defence or Prosecution, as a principle should be met. But I'd like to hear from Mr. Harvey and Mr. Emmerson whether they take a similar position as Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So do I, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this matter having been practically resolved. This also -- Mr. Guy-Smith, the remaining issue on the agenda was outstanding requests. Could we assume on the basis of the information the Chamber received that the Chamber is aware of these requests and that to the extent UNMIK has not yet responded, that a response will be given. I mean, is my word as a rubber stamp in this meeting would serve the same purpose, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I just want to clarify that the reference to the rubber stamp or to any kind of initialing was intended to give UNMIK comfort that some official channel that is aware of this happening, because otherwise we open ourselves up to numerous requests from the general public that are not related, for instance, to a proceeding. So the fact that there is any annotation is useful for recording purposes and is useful as a minimum screen, and that's all we're asking for, and the rest is fine, understood. On the issue of the pending statements, you have our word, Your Honour, that UNMIK devotes priority to these requests and if there's the required information specificity, we are able to address them in -- as quickly as we possibly can. And you have our commitment that these will be addressed very, very promptly in the coming days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let me just see what remains on the agenda as far as UNMIK is concerned. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, just as one last housekeeping matter with regard to the pending requests. I'm not sure whether or not it would be of any assistance in the event such documentation exists for an inventory of those requests that have been -- previously been made by the OTP probably about the same subject matter to become either part of some private or confidential record because one of the things that I don't want to be doing is duplicating those efforts that have already been made by the Office of the Prosecutor with regard to those outstanding files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course there is another matter that just as I earlier said that the Prosecution should not be kept informed about any discovery effort by the Defence, perhaps the Defence would not be entitled to follow every step in the discovery in the investigation. But of course if it is related to one of your earlier requests, then, Mr. Re, you're invited perhaps to provide the Defence with any of the follow-up steps to make an inventory of on what requests you made, what effort, and what response you received, if not yet disclosed to the Defence. I mean, it's now mainly cleaning our desk and going for the future rather than anything else. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's helpful, I think that UNMIK could also be of assistance in this regard. We do have an inventory of each and every request that was submitted to us and the status of the request and any conditions that may have been given in responding to such requests. So we could, not immediately but in the coming days, perhaps share with the Defence and with the Prosecution an inventory of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would not have asked you to do that, to be the instrument of verification on what actually happened until now. At the same time, since you're offering it by your own, I'm -- I'm inclined to be happy with your offer. Mr. Re, you haven't expressed yourself on the matter, but I take it that in our effort to clear our desks you would not oppose or would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, there's a lot to be said generally for desk clearing, but I would like to speak of course to UNMIK and just to check the terms of what we've -- of the correspondence between UNMIK and the Prosecution before we'd agree to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- a blanket disclosure to the Defence of diplomatic letters between the government authority and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think what Mr. Guy-Smith is seeking and what is offered by UNMIK is that whenever a request was made by the Defence which has been given follow-up by the OTP and then another follow-up by UNMIK, that the Defence is informed through an inventory by what was done. Whatever is outside the scope of what the Defence asked for is, of course, a matter between OTP and UNMIK, unless of course there are any disclosure obligations resulting from those matters. But that's not what Mr. Guy-Smith is focusing on. Within these limits, Mr. Re, would you agree that this would be a very practical solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If we're talking about an index of when we asked UNMIK for material and when they responded, we don't object to an index of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And also on when UNMIK responded and perhaps going as far as whether any material was attached without -- it seems that the parties agree on the matter and that they have, I take it, with gratitude accepted UNMIK's offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Most definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then there -- are there any other issues at this moment? Would this include -- Mr. Harvey, I'm looking at you. I know that you are desperately seeking for asylum files. Would these be covered in your view at least - and perhaps I should inform the UNMIK representatives. Mr. Harvey would very much like to know from a number of witnesses whether any asylum requests have been made and whether UNMIK has any copies of these asylum requests and could provide them. It is a kind of material which is slightly different from what one would usually expect. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour for nurturing my request here in this way. If I could just make it clear to our friends from UNMIK the purpose here. Essentially, there are witnesses who have, of course, made statements in connection with this case who have sought asylum or relocation to other countries and who may well have sought the assistance of UNMIK in doing so. We are not interested in where they've gone, why they've gone there specifically; what we're interested in is whether the -- they made any statements in the form of a sworn affidavit or anything of a similar nature which refer to the crimes that are alleged against the accused in this case. In other words, that they are seeking relocation because on such and such a date they were present at or their family member was a victim of a particular crime, and for that reason they are, therefore, in fear. Conversely, of course, if they made statements claiming asylum and failed to make any reference to matters which we would -- or the Tribunal would reasonably expect to be included, then that is a matter of enormous significance as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before UNMIK responds --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- can I just indicate that this isn't a matter which directly concerns the Prosecution. It may tangentially, but it is an interest in which we submit the Victims and Witnesses Section of the registry of the ICTY may have an interest and should be heard before that matter is taken up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is another matter involved, Mr. Harvey, and that's the following: UNMIK, I would say, has certain responsibilities in providing security to the citizens of Kosovo. If someone seeks asylum elsewhere, that might well include a statement of unsufficient protection provided by the state where he lives at that moment. To that extent, it could not be excluded that UNMIK also has a kind of a personal interest in the matter, but also there let's be very practical. The first question, of course, would be whether UNMIK keeps any record of such request, because if the answer is no, we don't have to further explore what the position of UNMIK would be and whether an order should be given or should not be given, what interests are involved. If the representative of UNMIK could immediately answer that question, then of course our -- could be that the matter is perhaps not resolved, but at least from our desk at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, to my knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORG-OLIVIER
utterances.text: -- and there is no sort of central unit within UNMIK that has this information. If individuals that have concerns, you know, register their concerns with police, these would not necessarily come to the head of UNMIK for any kind of involvement. Possibly the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees which deals with these matters is in a better position to sort of provide us with some information. We could check and see if there's any information that could be of any value, but UNMIK does not pursue these matters or does not have any pool of information that could be of any value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's one. Mr. Harvey, another category was not those who are seeking asylum but those who are seeking relocation. Well, there is another -- at least another problem might be involved, that is seeking relocation is usually when persons have fear that their testimony in the case could cause them -- that could cause them damage, in whatever way, which need to be avoided by putting them to another place. And now you say, I'm not interested in where they are, I'm not interested -- I'm just interested in their stories. I think it certainly would need further consultation with the Victims and Witnesses Section before we further deal with the matter, and of course we could contact the Victims and Witnesses Section and try to have a similar exercise and see whether we could reach practical solutions. But there again I would say if you could, perhaps with the reference to the transcript of today, contact the Victims and Witnesses Section and find out what their position would be in relation to disclosure of such limited information, that might assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I haven't got the documents in front of me at the moment, but since this slightly tangential issue has been raised, we have already and some considerable time ago first approached the Prosecution and through the Prosecution the Victims and Witnesses Unit in respect of a particular upcoming witness and the issue of relocation. And obviously we made the position clear that we were not interested in the details of where a person had been relocated to, but certainly in the jurisdiction in which I practice, it would be regarded as highly relevant material if particular arrangements, for example, financial arrangements, have been made which might influence a witness's motivates for making themselves available as a witness in the first place. It may be a fact irrelevant. The Victims and Witnesses Unit's position was -- and as I say, I don't have the with wording in front of me, so with that caveat, it was essentially fairly uncompromising [Realtime transcript read in error "compromising"] on the face of it, and so it may be that some process of the kind that we've gone through today will in due course be necessary in respect of the VWS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not necessarily from what I understand from you, Mr. Borg-Olivier, UNMIK as far as is known at this moment, doesn't keep records of the kind Mr. Harvey is seeking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, if I could just pursue that a moment. I do understand Mr. Borg-Olivier to be saying there is no office or unit within UNMIK that is charged with this specific responsibility. It may be that there -- if we were to provide a list of individual names to UNMIK and ask -- it may be a question of how files are accessed, and I'm thinking that if we were to provide a list of individual names to UNMIK, they would be able to indicate to us whether there may be anything on their files of the nature that we have been discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think -- it's a very delicate issue, relocation and asylum. As you may know that usually if someone seeks asylum that the state where he comes from is usually not informed of the reasons. So therefore it's really a very delicate question. I think not much is lost if you provide UNMIK with a list of the names, but by saying this, the Chamber does not express any opinion, any further opinion on what the obligations would be, what kind of invitations or orders the Chamber would issue if UNMIK would have reservations or doubts as whether to provide any of the information. I draw the attention, however, of UNMIK to the fact that providing material under Rule 70 could also be providing material to the Defence under Rule 70. They could use that -- Rule 70 is not limited to material provided to the Prosecution, and the Chamber has no reason whatsoever to even consider at this moment that the Defence teams would not act in full conformity with their professional obligations and duties. This -- Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm merely standing since you were addressing me before, but I would say -- I would thank you for those remarks and we will certainly follow-up to UNMIK with a specific letter detailing our request, and then at least they may be able to notify us whether or not as a threshold issue there may exist any documents that may be of assistance. And then we can take it from there. Secondly, in relation to the Victims and Witnesses Unit, we will certainly draw to their attention the relevant passage of the transcript from today and see whether or not that may trigger any further response. But I would endorse Mr. Emmerson's suggestion that probably the most effective way is for the Chamber to entertain a similar hearing with them so that we can resolve this issue expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And whilst we're on the transcript in that regard, I note that page 43, lines 18 to 21, my submissions are recorded as having described the position of the Victims and Witnesses Unit on this issue as compromising, and in fact the word I used, was "uncompromising."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how we understood it. That's the only way it made sense, as a matter of fact. Is there any issue further, because I don't want to take any further of your time. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just on that last issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution make it quite clear that if there's any -- or any request made of UNMIK concerning any Prosecution witnesses or potential witnesses or people the Prosecution has taken statements from who may have made applications for asylum or relocation, we want to be informed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- of that, because we will want to be heard before that's taken any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Re has copies of our requests already in relation to each of those witnesses so nothing here will be of any surprise to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that will be the same in the future so that Mr. Re is always aware that if any information is sought in relation to any of the potential Prosecution witnesses, that is those who are on the list of witnesses or would it also include ever person you ever interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's the latter because there clearly are some people who may have been relocated or protective measures have been taken but they didn't ultimately make it to the witness list. Our concern is information relating to relocation or asylum applications, as opposed to the more generic information which the Defence is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The request is now --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- about to request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
